channel.description: Utah breaking news and local top stories from KSL.com

item.title: Utah may increase awareness of its laws targeting left-lane loafing violations
item.description: Utah Highway Patrol Col. Greg Holley told the Legislature's Transportation Interim Committee last week that troopers often face a dilemma when drivers linger in the left lane rather than passing and moving back over, since state law targets both that "left-lane loafing" and aggressive tailgating, and officers generally prioritize stopping the aggressive driver. UHP has averaged more than 500 impeding citations and over 3,000 HOV violations annually over the past three years, and Holley believes better public education, rather than heavier enforcement, could ease the conflict. The Utah Department of Transportation has already posted nearly 50 signs telling trucks to stay out of the left lanes and more than 60 reminding slower traffic to keep right, and officials floated adding messaging to overhead digital signs plus a social media push similar to its recent zipper-merge campaign. Rep. Kay Christofferson, R-Lehi, the committee's co-chair, said many drivers seem to zone out in the left lane without realizing they should yield to passing traffic. Any messaging changes would come later, but Holley said UHP will keep enforcing the existing law, including periodic left-lane-impeding enforcement blitzes.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams

item.title: Man who supplied gun found guilty of murder in Cedar City jury trial
item.description: A Fifth District Court jury convicted 24-year-old Matthew Sorber-Petrie of murder, five counts of felony discharge of a firearm causing injury, and obstruction of justice, following a shooting near Cedar City on January 17, 2025, that killed 18-year-old KayLee Dutton and injured a passenger. Prosecutors argued Sorber-Petrie was criminally liable as an accomplice because he supplied the gun to two other men, knowing they intended to use it, after roughly a dozen shots were fired into the truck Dutton was driving. Those two shooters, Ethan Galloway and Michael Hess-Witacki, previously pleaded guilty to murder and were each sentenced last September to 15 years to life plus additional consecutive terms; a fourth man, Aldric Felipe, received probation. Jurors deliberated about two and a half hours before returning their verdict, acquitting Sorber-Petrie on two additional firearm counts; he is due back before Judge Meb Anderson for sentencing on September 29.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft

item.title: Roy teen shows signs of recovery after being hit by car while riding e-scooter
item.description: 14-year-old Tucker of Roy suffered serious head, body and internal injuries along with several broken bones after being struck by a car while riding his e-scooter through a crosswalk near 5600 South and 2700 West shortly after 8 p.m. Wednesday. He was airlifted to Primary Children's Hospital, where his mother, Alicia Griffith, said doctors weren't initially sure he would wake up, but he is now awake, talking and showing signs of recovery, with hope he could be released as soon as this weekend. The driver is cooperating with the investigation. Griffith, who said "he should have died," has used the scare to urge greater helmet use and driver awareness around scooter riders, and friends and family have started a fundraiser to help cover medical costs.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon

item.title: USU, Hi Tech Solutions to develop nuclear training, research campus in Brigham City
item.description: Nuclear company Hi Tech Solutions, Utah State University and Brigham City signed a memorandum of understanding to build a nuclear training and research campus aimed at growing the region's nuclear workforce. The campus would offer technical certification, apprenticeships and applied research facilities, with USU handling curriculum and a long-term land lease, Brigham City managing site planning, and Hi Tech Solutions serving as master developer. The move follows the company's November announcement with Holtec International to build several small modular reactors around Brigham City, and comes as Gov. Spencer Cox and House Speaker Mike Schultz have pushed nuclear power as part of the state's "Operation Gigawatt" energy strategy. USU President Brad Mortensen said the partnership would prepare students for high-demand careers while supporting the state's energy and national-security goals.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich

item.title: Utah has scores of public high schools — which one is No. 1?
item.description: U.S. News & World Report's newly released annual rankings name Karl G. Maeser Preparatory Academy, a Lindon charter school founded in 2007, as Utah's top public high school, with a score of 97.78 out of 100. The rankings, covering nearly 18,000 public high schools nationwide, weigh factors including state assessment performance, AP/IB exam participation and success, graduation rates and college readiness; Tennessee's Central Magnet School topped the national list. Maeser Prep director Katie Wirig and executive director Robyn Ellis credited the school's emphasis on rigorous, Socratic-style discussion, extensive graduation requirements and programs like its January "Winterim" seminar and senior capstone projects. Other Utah schools landing just outside the state's top 10 included Beehive Science and Technology Academy, Bingham High School, Salt Lake Center for Science Education and Lone Peak High School.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen

item.title: 5 years after Gabby Petito's disappearance, her story continues to drive change
item.description: Five years after Gabby Petito's 2021 disappearance and death -- she vanished at 22 while traveling with fiancé Brian Laundrie and was later found dead in Wyoming in a killing ruled a homicide -- her case is still shaping domestic violence policy. Attorney Steve Jensen of Parker & McConkie, who represents the Petito family, said the family has channeled the attention on Gabby's case into lasting change rather than animosity, pointing to Utah's 2023 SB117 law requiring officers responding to domestic violence calls to use a lethality assessment and connect high-risk victims to an emergency shelter hotline. Similar lethality-assessment laws have since spread to states including Florida and New York, and the family founded the Gabby Petito Foundation to support victims and raise awareness of warning signs. Jensen said policy change takes time but that education remains critical, while separately the family's wrongful-death lawsuit against the Moab City Police Department -- which denies wrongdoing over its handling of a domestic violence incident involving the couple weeks before Gabby's death -- remains pending, with the Utah Supreme Court expected to set oral arguments soon on the family's appeal.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson

item.title: Flooding at Bryce Canyon spurs rescue efforts
item.description: Heavy monsoon flooding hit Bryce Canyon National Park on Monday afternoon, prompting rescue crews to pull 11 people from four separate trails -- Fairyland, Navajo Loop, Peekaboo and Queen's Garden -- between roughly 2:30 and 5:30 p.m. Two hikers were treated for hypothermia symptoms while others were evaluated on-scene and released, according to Garfield County Sheriff's Office spokesman Wade Mathews. State Route 12 was briefly closed because of the flooding before reopening, and the park reported trail damage from the runoff. About 15-20 responders from Garfield EMS, park rangers and the sheriff's office worked the rescues, at times slowed by lightning in the area, and Mathews said some longtime residents told him they'd never seen that much water coming out of the canyon.
item.dc:creator: Payton Davis

item.title: Judge gives man consecutive sentences for 'horrendous' double killing at party
item.description: A Third District judge sentenced Patrocinio Perez, 24, to consecutive prison terms totaling at least 30 years for opening fire at a house party in Magna in August 2021, killing 18-year-old Ivan Valenzuela and 19-year-old Juan Valentine Rodriguez and wounding a 17-year-old girl. Judge Heather Brereton handed down 15 years to life on two aggravated murder counts plus three additional five-years-to-life terms for discharging a firearm. Deputy Salt Lake County Attorney Vincent Meister told the court the shooting was an unprovoked ambush with no warning, while Perez, represented by attorney Rudy Bautista, apologized and said he knew what he did was wrong. Brereton told Perez she hoped he understood the lasting consequences his actions have had on others, five years after the shooting.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft

item.title: Lehi boy home recovering after 2-story window fall
item.description: Six-year-old Zion Silva fell from a second-story window at his grandparents' house in Saratoga Springs on Aug. 15 after a window screen gave way while he and his 4-year-old brother, Leo, were looking out to spot cousins arriving. Zion suffered a fractured skull, a broken collarbone and a forehead laceration requiring stitches, and was airlifted to Primary Children's Hospital, where he spent seven days as doctors watched for infection risk near his brain. His parents, Carlos and Becca Silva, said Leo later told them Zion had pushed him back from the window just before falling, which the family believes may have kept his brother from also going through. Zion is now recovering at home and is due for a follow-up MRI in three months, while a GoFundMe has been set up to help with medical costs.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell

item.title: Alleged pay dispute leads to shooting, charges in Sanpete County
item.description: Mario Almanza Valencia, 61, of Mt. Pleasant, was booked into Sanpete County Jail and charged Monday in 6th District Court with attempted murder and obstruction of justice after allegedly confronting someone over an unpaid debt and firing a .22-caliber rifle at the person multiple times in Fayette on Friday night. Charging documents say Valencia, visibly intoxicated, pointed the rifle at the victim's head at one point, but the victim ducked and the shots missed; neighbors who witnessed the confrontation called 911. Responding officers found Valencia in his vehicle with a flat tire, smelling of alcohol and marijuana, slurring his speech and stumbling, and his own son reportedly confirmed by phone that his father had been drinking. Valencia also faces charges including discharging a firearm, drug possession, refusing a chemical test, carrying a weapon while intoxicated and having an open container of alcohol.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy

item.title: Sen. John Curtis weighs in on the future of the SAVE America Act
item.description: Utah Sen. John Curtis says he supports requiring voter ID and proof of citizenship but is skeptical the broader SAVE America Act -- which would also force states to hand over complete voter rolls to the federal government and restrict mail-in ballots -- can realistically pass before November, and he'd rather see a narrower bill focused just on ID and citizenship checks. Fellow Utah Sen. Mike Lee has pushed Congress to skip its August recess to get the legislation through, while President Trump has argued Republicans could lock in decades of election wins if the Senate filibuster were scrapped to pass it -- a framing Curtis said makes it harder to win over Democratic support. Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, the state's chief election officer, has separately criticized the administration's push to restrict mail-in voting. The push comes as the U.S. Supreme Court has allowed the administration to implement new voter-eligibility lists, even as a nationwide injunction still blocks a related USPS mail-ballot rule and other legal fights continue.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko

item.title: Washington Terrace presses 'pause' on Flock cameras
item.description: Washington Terrace, in Weber County, has halted a three-month trial of Flock license-plate-reader cameras it had been running. Mayor Mark Allen said he decided to put the brakes on it after Gov. Spencer Cox recently floated a possible privacy audit of the technology at his monthly news conference, and that he believes he has the support of the full city council. Allen said dozens of residents cheered the move on social media, and he framed the issue as needing "a balance between freedom and safety." The pause isn't necessarily permanent -- the city council is set to discuss the matter further at its Sept. 1 meeting, leaving open the possibility the cameras could return.
item.dc:creator: Britt Johnson

item.title: Utah's first public via ferrata course draws thousands of people to Vernal
item.description: North America's largest public via ferrata -- a climbing route where visitors clip into fixed steel cables and climb rebar rungs bolted into cliff faces -- has opened at Ashley Gorge near Vernal, funded by the Access Utah Foundation to boost outdoor tourism in the area. Dyno Outfitters owner Amber Toler began guiding groups through the roughly 3-4 mile course during a fall 2025 soft opening ahead of an April 2026 grand opening, and waiver records show thousands of people have completed it since. Operations director Jasmynn States said the growing popularity has brought safety concerns, since some visitors show up with improper gear, warning that clipping into the wall "doesn't necessarily mean that it's safe" and that a fall could cause serious spine or organ injury. Visitors like Layton's Jason Johnson, who came with friends to try the route, said it's worth doing with the right equipment and guides. Via ferrata routes date back to World War I in Italy's Dolomite mountains, and gear rentals are available on-site for those without their own equipment.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson

item.title: Monsoons lit up Utah's sky with a rare type of rainbow
item.description: Utah's monsoon storms produced rare "moonbows," or lunar rainbows, visible Sunday night in spots including Rich County, Garden City, Park City and Rockport Reservoir. Moonbows form when moonlight rather than sunlight refracts through raindrops at the right angle, requiring the moon to sit lower than about 42 degrees in the sky; this weekend's moon was 74-82% illuminated, which NOAA says can still be bright enough to produce a faint moonbow even without a full moon. Rich County resident Corey Wiley was among those who captured and shared a photo of the phenomenon. KSL meteorologists note more moonbows are possible as monsoon moisture lingers, with additional scattered storms forecast for Monday and possibly Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams

item.title: 2 accused in southern Utah of Flock camera vandalism
item.description: Two young men, ages 18 and 19, were arrested after allegedly cutting down and smashing a Flock license-plate-reader camera at 410 S. Main St. in Kanarraville, Iron County, early Monday. A witness reported hearing a Sawzall and watching the pair cut the camera at its base, damage its solar panel and sever wires before fleeing; Cedar City police later found a sledgehammer and a Sawzall blade hidden in trash bags in the suspects' vehicle. One of the men reportedly told investigators he got the idea after watching "de-flock America" videos on social media, and both now face charges of criminal mischief and obstruction of justice. The arrest comes amid a broader wave of Flock camera vandalism nationally and as Gov. Spencer Cox has ordered a state review of the cameras over privacy concerns, even though police departments along the Wasatch Front, which use hundreds of the devices, say they're valuable investigative tools.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy

item.title: The first lawsuit has been filed over feds' new plan for Lake Powell and Lake Mead
item.description: Nevada, the Colorado River Commission of Nevada and the Southern Nevada Water Authority sued the U.S. Department of the Interior on Monday over its newly signed Post-2026 Colorado River Operations plan. The 10-year plan, signed Friday by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, adjusts water allocations every two years starting in 2027-2028 to keep Lake Powell near 3,510 feet, and requires roughly 1.25 million acre-feet of annual cuts from Lower Basin states while sparing Upper Basin states including Utah. Nevada argues the cuts are unfair and would slash its allocation to about 86,500 acre-feet a year -- a 60% drop from 2024 usage -- with Gov. Joe Lombardo calling it "a matter of survival" for the roughly two-thirds of Nevadans served by that water. The suit, filed in federal court, is the first legal challenge to the new plan. The Colorado River Authority of Utah said it is still reviewing the lawsuit and had no immediate comment.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams

item.title: Weber School District's new Catalyst Campus gives students a head start on careers
item.description: Weber School District is launching a new Catalyst Campus offering hands-on career education across eight pathways, including health sciences, computer science, engineering, design and entrepreneurship. The program, led by Innovation High principal Nikki Slaw and CTE director Rod Belknap, has lined up partnerships with more than 60 local industries so students can work directly with professionals on real-world projects. Students can take part while staying enrolled at their home schools or by attending full-time. A dedicated new building is slated to break ground in September, with the full campus expected to be operating in roughly three years. Belknap said working with an industry partner on something like a real-life website gives students a deeper kind of learning experience than a typical classroom project.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer

item.title: Saratoga Springs teen charged with killing mother, brother
item.description: A 16-year-old Saratoga Springs boy has been charged with two counts of aggravated murder and obstruction of justice in the March 27, 2025 deaths of his mother, 44-year-old Jessica Orton Lyman, and his 8-year-old half-brother, Eli Painter, and prosecutors are seeking to try him as an adult. The two were found dead in Lyman's bedroom the next morning. Charging documents cite home surveillance video capturing an argument and three gunshots around midnight, footage of a masked figure matching the teen's height and build near the home a few hours later, gunshot residue on his clothing, scratches on his shoulder, and his DNA under a victim's fingernails and on his mother's shorts; investigators also found a handwritten note in his room referencing a "murder story" and types of forensic evidence. Saratoga Springs Police Chief Andrew Burton called it "a very complex case" that required an extraordinary amount of time and attention to detail. If convicted as an adult, the teen would face a mandatory minimum of 25 years to life in prison.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy

item.title: Impaired, unlicensed driver allegedly caused head-on crash near Park City
item.description: Jonathan Casimiro Abarca Rodriguez, 26, was arrested after allegedly driving drunk and unlicensed into oncoming traffic near Kearns Boulevard and Round Valley Drive close to Park City on Saturday night, striking a Subaru head-on. Three people in the Subaru were hurt, one seriously, while Rodriguez and a passenger fled on foot across a fence into a field before being caught. Police say his blood-alcohol level measured 0.277% -- more than five times the legal limit -- and his car held multiple open containers of alcohol; he admitted to drinking "several beers." Rodriguez, who had never held a driver's license and was subject to an alcohol restriction after a prior 2025 DUI conviction in Murray, now faces more than 16 charges including DUI, four counts of negligently operating a vehicle causing injury, reckless driving and three counts of leaving the scene of a serious-injury crash. He was booked into Summit County Jail.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy

item.title: 100-year-old WWII veteran honored at Delta-Millard rivalry game
item.description: Delta High School honored 100-year-old veteran Staff Sgt. Ken Porter as honorary flag bearer at Friday night's Delta-Millard rivalry football game. Porter volunteered for the U.S. Army Air Force at age 17 in 1944, one of six Delta teens to do so, and served as a tail gunner on a B-17 bomber, flying more than 50 missions and logging over 270 combat flight hours during World War II. School announcer Rob Jeffery organized the tribute after learning of Porter's service, telling the crowd the teens "weren't even old enough to vote" when they went to fight. Porter said he was honored to return to the football field "at my age" and reflected that he served to keep the country the way it should be so everyone could enjoy moments like the game.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone

item.title: Tyler Robinson's case 'should not be made into a reality TV show,' attorneys argue
item.description: Attorneys for Tyler Robinson, 23, are asking a Provo judge to keep cameras out of his Sept. 1 hearing in 4th District Court, arguing media coverage at this stage could taint the jury pool. Robinson faces capital murder and six other charges over the Sept. 10, 2025 campus shooting death of conservative activist Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University, and prosecutors have said they'll seek the death penalty if he's convicted. The defense's filing opposes camera requests from the Salt Lake Tribune and KUTV, contending the case "should not be made into a reality TV show" and that a preliminary hearing relies on largely unreliable hearsay rather than trial-ready evidence. Judge Tony Graf, who presided over a week-long preliminary hearing in July, has previously denied Robinson's objections to electronic media coverage. Separately, an attorney for Kirk's family has asked that all evidence presented at the hearing be made public.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy

item.title: 3-year college degrees grow more popular in the US, saving time and cash. But critics aren't sold
item.description: Reduced-credit bachelor's programs requiring as few as 90 credit hours -- rather than the traditional 120 -- are now offered in at least 26 states as of spring 2026, letting students finish in about three years. Utah's Ensign College in Salt Lake City was an early adopter after the Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities approved the model in 2023, alongside Brigham Young University-Idaho; students like laid-off web developer Giles Sims say the faster path helps them re-enter the workforce while supporting a family. Proponents such as University of Pennsylvania's Robert Zemsky, who first pitched three-year degrees in 2009 and revived the idea in 2022 through the College-in-3 Exchange, frame it as a way to cut costs -- one Mount Mary University student expects to save about $20,000. But critics including American Association of University Professors president Todd Wolfson call the approach "cutting corners" rather than genuine innovation, warning it could narrow students' education, confuse employers and graduate schools, and complicate licensure in fields with strict credit requirements. Higher-education historian John Thelin notes the four-year model itself is a 19th-century convention rather than any fixed standard.
item.dc:creator: Heather Hollingsworth

item.title: Alpine Church Logan campus prepares for grand opening
item.description: The Alpine Church in Logan is preparing for the grand opening of a new building at 91 East 2440 North in North Logan, set for Sept. 20, after outgrowing its previous site on South Main Street. Pastor John Belles said the old location could only support three Sunday services with overflow parking blocks away, prompting the move to a spot about four miles north with better parking. On the first two services held at the new building Aug. 16, roughly 650 people attended combined, according to pastoral team member Steve Rodriguez, who said volunteers scrambled to finish preparations just in time. Belles said he wants to avoid becoming a "mega-church" and would instead launch additional campuses, potentially in Hyrum, if the new site outgrows its space -- Alpine Church already runs six locations across Cache, Box Elder, Weber and Davis counties. The church has since rearranged seating to improve traffic flow ahead of the official grand-opening celebration.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr

item.title: From supercomputers to startups: Inside Utah's growing bet on AI
item.description: Utah is making a major push into artificial intelligence on multiple fronts, anchored by the University of Utah's new $50 million Redtail supercomputer, which ranks 160th fastest in the world and 5th among U.S. public universities. Manish Parashar, the university's first chief AI officer, is overseeing efforts that also include an $18.6 million Health AI Vault for cancer and medical research and a spot in the NSF's AI-driven Cloud Laboratories network. State government is investing too, with a $100 million Pro-Human AI Initiative and new laws championed by Margaret Woolley Busse's Office of AI Policy covering deepfakes, high-risk AI disclosures and mental health safeguards. Meanwhile Utah AI startups are pulling in venture capital, including an $80 million round for Parker Ence's Jump AI, a $97 million round for Databento, and $115 million for Zanskar, while Silicon Slopes has launched a "Start School" program to build the state's AI talent pipeline.
item.dc:creator: Brooke Nally

item.title: Utah approves 3 more productions projected to bring $9.3M economic impact
item.description: The Utah Board of Tourism Development approved state incentives for three film productions on Friday, projecting a combined $9.3 million economic impact and more than 100 jobs across shoots in Washington, Kane, Uintah, Iron, and Utah counties. The approvals include an eighth season of History Channel's "The Secret of Skinwalker Ranch," a Kane and Washington counties shoot for "The Last Treasure Hunt," and an untitled feature from director Robert Machoian set to film this fall. Utah Film Commission director Virginia Pearce touted the approvals, noting the state has now backed more than 30 productions in the past year and has 29 counties equipped to support filming. The incentives come through Utah's Motion Picture Incentive Program, which requires 75% Utah residents in cast and crew and 75% of production days in rural Utah in exchange for up to a 25% refundable tax credit, and the smaller-scale Community Film Incentive Program, which offers up to a 20% cash rebate for productions with 85% Utah residents on staff.
item.dc:creator: Margaret Darby

item.title: Would you feel safer knowing an armed civilian was nearby?
item.description: As mass shootings have grown more frequent nationally, this piece examines the debate over armed civilians intervening during attacks, noting that personal protection now motivates 72% of gun owners, up from 67% in 2017. It highlights Jordan Salinas, who trained for active-shooter scenarios after Boise's 2021 mall shooting and later stopped a gunman at a Twin Falls, Idaho, In-N-Out Burger on Aug. 1, credited with limiting casualties. James Keith, director of the ALERRT training program at Texas State University, said his group teaches an "Avoid, Deny, Defend" approach that treats armed resistance as a last resort, since civilians who intervene risk crossfire or being mistaken for the attacker by police -- citing the deaths of Johnny Hurley in Colorado in 2021 and Jemel Roberson in 2018. The article also references a pending Utah wrongful-death lawsuit over Matthew Alder, accused of recklessly firing a gun and killing Afa Ah Loo at a Salt Lake City protest in June 2025. Keith urged situational awareness and having an exit plan rather than living in fear, saying such violence "can happen anywhere."
item.dc:creator: Emma Pitts

item.title: The world's largest collection of outdoor gear designs is at a Utah university
item.description: Utah State University's Outdoor Recreation Archive, curated by Clint Pumphrey and co-archivist Chase Anderson, has grown from about 250 outdoor brand catalogues collected starting in 2017 into the world's largest public collection of outdoor gear catalogues, magazines and design sketches, representing more than 1,000 brands and now expanding into ski and climbing films. An Instagram account Anderson started in 2019 helped the archive draw global attention and donations, including personal sketchbooks from JanSport co-founder Skip Yowell, retrieved from his widow's basement in Kansas after his 2015 death. The account has become the most-followed Utah State University page behind the university's main account, and the collection travels internationally for exhibits, with stops planned in Taiwan and Portland, Oregon. Anderson said the archive's emphasis on public access, including open reading hours that draw visitors from as far as Tokyo, sets it apart, though he noted a gap in materials from Utah-based outdoor companies that the team is actively working to fill.
item.dc:creator: Bryanna Willis

item.title: Utah voters turn on incumbents as statewide approval ratings drop into the red
item.description: A Deseret News/Hinckley Institute of Politics poll of nearly 800 registered Utah voters found an anti-incumbent mood pulling down approval for the state's top elected officials, with Gov. Spencer Cox's rating falling underwater for the first time as governor: down from 51% to 41% approval since January while disapproval climbed to 49%. Sen. Mike Lee's approval also flipped from 47%-37% in February to 39%-46% by August, and Sen. John Curtis and the Utah Legislature likewise slid into negative territory. Hinckley Institute director Jason Perry pointed to a mix of factors including a shaky economy, high gas prices and cost of living, while state Sen. Todd Weiler tied much of Cox's decline to backlash over the Stratos data center project in Box Elder County, which also contributed to former Senate President Stuart Adams losing his June primary. Cox, who has said he won't seek a third term, continues to push depolarization efforts even as his support among independents and Democrats has eroded sharply. None of the officials polled are on the ballot in this November's midterms.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco

item.title: Sunset memorial coming together to honor Vietnam War victims of Agent Orange
item.description: Larry Kerr, a 78-year-old Vietnam veteran from Syracuse battling health effects of Agent Orange, is leading an effort with the Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation to build a memorial at Sunset City Veterans Memorial Park honoring victims of the herbicide. Part of the memorial, including a large orange granite slab and two informational panels on the Vietnam War and Agent Orange, has already been installed, with Kerr hoping for completion within weeks and a possible unveiling ceremony around Veterans Day, Nov. 11. Sunset Mayor Scott Wiggill praised the project and said it could become one of the largest Agent Orange memorials in the country. The memorial notes that roughly 750,000 U.S. veterans have died from Agent Orange exposure and also acknowledges service members affected by burn pits and other toxic exposures from more recent conflicts. Wiggill sees the memorial adding to the area's existing military history sites, including Hill Air Force Base, the Hill Aerospace Museum and the Layton Vietnam Memorial Wall Replica.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack

item.title: Utah teen recovering after serious beach accident leaves him with broken neck
item.description: Utah teenager Gunnar Olsen broke his neck diving into a wave during a beach outing with friends, misjudging the surf after an earlier wave had already crashed, and was pulled from the water by lifeguards before being flown home to Primary Children's Hospital. His parents, who learned of the accident by text while leaving a cancer treatment appointment for his father Chad, say the injury has stunned a family already dealing with Chad's stage 4 cancer diagnosis. Friends, including longtime friend Oakley Peterson, have rallied around Gunnar with visits and created an Instagram page, "Stronger With Gunnar," to share updates and raise money. Doctors say it will take several months for spinal swelling to subside before Gunnar's long-term prognosis becomes clearer, though he has already begun regaining some movement. His mother, Marni Olsen, says the family is taking recovery "one day at a time" and is grateful for the community support.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen

item.title: Visitors spent a record $13.7B in Utah's economy last year, report finds
item.description: A University of Utah Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute report found Utah's tourism economy generated a record $13.7 billion in economic impact in 2025, a 0.6% inflation-adjusted increase over 2024 that produced $1.6 billion in direct state and local tax revenue and supported roughly a tenth of the state's jobs. The gain came despite declines in hotel occupancy, park visitation, airport passenger traffic, and a sharp drop in visitors from Canada (-22%) and China (-23%), partly attributed to tariff-related boycotts and a weak ski season with 4.8 million skier visits, down 26% amid record-low snowpack. Growth areas included downtown Salt Lake City hotel and event activity, a 5.9% jump in dining spending, and a 17% rise in spectator-sports tourism jobs tied to the Utah Mammoth and other new teams. Report author Jennifer Leaver said the results show the industry "moving into a more normalized environment rather than a broad-based downturn," while Utah Office of Tourism and Film managing director Natalie Randall credited statewide partnerships for the record impact. The report projects modest growth in 2026 travel, aided by events like the FIFA World Cup, but flags inflation and interest-rate uncertainty as risks.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams

item.title: From salsa and chips to owning a market: How a southern Utah couple supports local businesses
item.description: Harry and Summer Altena turned a 52-year-old family salsa recipe into the Pop's Chips brand and later expanded into yogurt with Dry Orchard, and for the past year they've run the Washington Farmer's Market at Veterans Park in Washington, Utah. The Saturday morning market, which grew out of an earlier Wednesday-evening concept, gives small vendors hands-on mentorship; 23-year-old vendor Daisy Mooy said the couple "made it super easy, and they just really wanted me to succeed." Beyond selling local goods, the market has partnered with six area animal shelters to facilitate 84 pet adoptions (63 dogs and 21 cats) and offers family activities like face painting, balloon artists, scavenger hunts, bingo, live music and playground access. Summer Altena said the goal is to make it easy for vendors to show up each week, noting "we know how hard it is to get it all together through the week and show up Saturday with a smile."
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown

item.title: 'Heartbroken': Tenants of Midvale apartments damaged in blaze press for help, answers
item.description: Dozens of tenants of the 220-unit North Union Apartments in Midvale, more than 160 units of which were damaged in a July 31 fire that burned for over 24 hours, rallied outside the complex Saturday demanding answers and help more than three weeks later. Tenants including Jeremy Seeley and Mia Miller said belongings like passports, jewelry and other valuables were lost or stolen, and that management, Keller Management, has failed to communicate or provide a clear plan for residents to retrieve items from the fourth floor, which sustained the heaviest damage. Protesters carried signs reading "Shame on Keller" and "Justice for NUA tenants," with several saying they were told by landlord agents they didn't need renters insurance and are now considering legal action; Keller Management did not immediately respond to KSL's request for comment. Unified Fire Authority investigators have said they suspect a mechanical issue in the attic caused the blaze, and while critical of the property's response, tenants like Savannah Page said the broader community and other apartment complexes have offered more support than North Union itself.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, Tim Vandenack

item.title: Holy Trinity Cathedral prepares for multi-million dollar renovations after 2020 earthquake
item.description: The Holy Trinity Cathedral of the Greek Orthodox Church in Salt Lake City, damaged by a 5.7-magnitude earthquake in March 2020, is preparing for a multi-million dollar seismic renovation. Parish council president George Karahalios said nearly 1,500 feet of interior cracks prompted a full seismic upgrade that will require stripping the century-old building down to brick, replacing its iconostasis, and installing a diaphragm beneath the dome so it can move during future quakes. The estimated cost has dropped from an initial $20-25 million to $16-18 million, with the church responsible for only about 10% since the building sits on the National Register of Historic Places; fundraising so far has reached just over $1 million toward that share. Past support has come from groups like the Huntsman Foundation and the annual Greek Festival, and Karahalios noted the church has also seen a rise in converts, with roughly 85 joining over the past year.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr

item.title: 'Shared artistic hobby': Mother-son duo showcases quilts at Springville Museum of Art
item.description: Jeri Schille and her son Colton Schille Smith are both showing quilts at the Springville Museum of Art's annual quilt show, likely the first mother-son pair exhibited together there. Schille, who learned from neighborhood mentors and had a quilter grandfather, entered a piece that took nearly 11 years to finish using the English paper piecing technique. Smith, who lives in North Carolina, took up the craft after getting a sewing machine for his 31st birthday in 2021, leaning on tutorials and FaceTime calls with his mother, and has made about 20 quilts in five years; his show entries include "Striped Lava Lamp" and "The I Spy Quilt," pieced from roughly 6,000 fabric scraps. Both described quilting as a bond that gave them a shared creative outlet across the distance between Utah and North Carolina.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom

item.title: The Full Circle Boys danced with Derek Hough. Now they're taking the stage at 'Dancing Under the Stars'
item.description: The Full Circle Boys, a five-member boy band of classically trained dancers, performed in the 21st annual "Dancing Under the Stars" showcase Aug. 21-22 at the SCERA Shell Outdoor Theatre in Orem. The group — Sean Garrity and James Herron of California, and Utahns Oliver Hincy, Dossan Bell and Jagger Moon, three of whom trained at Utah's Infinity Dance — recently wrapped a tour opening for Derek Hough on his inaugural Ovation Tour, where Moon said Hough became "our biggest cheerleader all year." Center Stage Performing Arts co-owner Kim DelGrosso said she believes the group is on the verge of a national breakthrough. The showcase featured about 20 dance numbers from area studios and groups, including the BYU Cougarettes and Polynesian dancers, according to SCERA president and CEO Adam Robertson.
item.dc:creator: Margaret Darby

item.title: The world's largest drinking chocolate library is coming to Utah
item.description: Knoops Chocolate, a UK-founded chain billed as the world's largest drinking chocolate library, opened its first U.S. storefront Saturday at 907 E. 900 South in Salt Lake City. Founder Jens Knoop, who grew up in Germany with a grandmother who served chocolate ceremonially, started the business in Rye, England in 2013 after struggling to find quality hot chocolate in London, sourcing cacao directly from farmers; the company now runs about 30 shops across the UK and Europe. The Utah shop offers 21 chocolate blends ranging from 28% white to 100% dark, letting customers pick their cacao percentage, temperature and texture, and adds a Utah-only PBFit peanut butter powder mix-in as what Knoop called a nod to local taste. Knoop said he expects the Salt Lake City launch to be "a big chocolate party" as the brand's introduction to the American market.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Gambles

item.title: Cedar Hills mom receiving double lung transplant after other cancer treatments fail
item.description: Kelsey Flake, a 39-year-old Cedar Hills mother of five, is undergoing a double lung transplant at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago after Stage 4 lung cancer returned in both lungs despite earlier chemotherapy, immunotherapy and a lobectomy; she now has just 41% lung capacity and needs full-time oxygen. She's enrolled in a Northwestern research program that is the only U.S. site offering double lung transplants to cancer patients, with all 17 prior participants (2021-2025) still alive versus under half of similarly staffed patients on medical therapy alone. A pre-transplant surgery to clear scar tissue was set for Thursday, after which she expects roughly a week's wait on the transplant list. Her five children, ages 6 to 15, are staying with grandparents in Cedar Hills during the school year and connect with her by nightly Zoom call, with plans to reunite by Christmas. Flake, who with her husband Jacob works in real estate, said getting out-of-network insurance approved felt like "a miracle," and the family has set up a GoFundMe while neighbors help with meals and household chores; doctors at Huntsman Cancer Institute are also studying a genetic variant several of her siblings share.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft

item.title: Man sent to prison for Millcreek stabbing over drug dispute
item.description: Joaquin "Chewy" Alvaro Sanchez, 47, was sentenced July 30 by 3rd District Court Judge Randall Skanchy to zero to five years in prison for aggravated assault after stabbing a man in a Millcreek apartment, with credit for 235 days already served. Police say the assault stemmed from a drug dispute that began Nov. 7, 2025, when Alvaro gave the victim methamphetamine and the man said he was pressured into distributing it but disposed of it instead, angering Alvaro. In a Nov. 22 voicemail, Alvaro said it was "about principle" that he would come after the man and his family, and days later allegedly confronted and stabbed him near 4150 S. 300 East, leaving a 5-inch laceration. Alvaro pleaded guilty May 21 under a plea deal that reduced the charge from a second-degree to a third-degree felony.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft

item.title: Utah's state parks recorded 12 million visits over past year. These ones are gaining popularity
item.description: More than 12.1 million people visited Utah state parks during fiscal year 2026, according to the Utah Division of State Parks, with visitation more than doubling over the past decade. Snow Canyon State Park posted the state's largest jump, up more than 162,000 visits (21%) to 919,545, while Utahraptor State Park in Grand County saw a roughly 390% surge to over 143,000 visits in its first full fiscal year since opening facilities in 2025; Wasatch Mountain and Goblin Valley state parks also climbed. Sand Hollow remained the most-visited park at over 1.4 million visits. Water-centric parks saw the steepest declines, led by Willard Bay (down more than 260,000 visits amid a reservoir-draining project) along with Jordanelle, Antelope Island, Rockport, Great Salt Lake Marina and Bear Lake, which division officials tied to Utah's record-low snowpack and reservoirs ending June at 68% capacity.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams

item.title: Too many kids 'on the sidelines': Utah 2034 pledges funds in youth sports donation effort
item.description: The Organizing Committee for the 2034 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games announced Saturday it will partner with the inaugural Utah Youth Sports Giving Day, a multi-week donation campaign running Sept. 12-26 to support Utah nonprofit sports organizations. Utah 2034 CEO Brad Wilson said too many underserved kids are left on the sidelines and called sport a powerful tool for building life skills, while Larry H. Miller Company CEO Steve Starks and Daniels Fund CEO Hanna Skandera Grady also spoke at the announcement event in South Jordan. Major donors including the Larry H. Miller Family Foundation, Daniels Fund, America First Credit Union and others have committed more than $1.5 million in matching funds, including a dollar-for-dollar match on the first $1 million raised, toward a $3 million campaign goal; the Colorado-born program has raised over $9 million there since 2024.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr

item.title: Massive new art installation planned for Sugar House seeks to highlight its neighbors
item.description: Salt Lake City officials announced Thursday that local artists Jeremy Morgan and Brooke Smart, working as Tomato Tomahto, will create "The People in Your Neighborhood," a seven-piece art installation for Fairmont Park and nearby McClelland Street in Sugar House. The pieces depict "familiar community figures," including kite-fliers, strolling families and joggers, and were chosen from 26 applicants for their "playful, community-centered approach." The project ties into a Fairmont Park renovation set to begin next year, funded through the city's $85 million 2022 parks bond, which set aside $441,000 for public art at various parks; the installation is expected to be fully in place by the end of 2028.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams

item.title: Evacuations lifted after Harley Fire reaches 75% containment
item.description: Evacuations for the Harley Fire near Garland in Box Elder County were lifted at 6:15 p.m. Saturday after Utah Fire Info reported the blaze reached 75% containment, according to Box Elder County Emergency Management. The fire, which broke out Friday in grass near I-15 and prompted a temporary highway closure, grew to 199 acres; residents near Harley Drive and the Radio Hill area can return to normal status.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr

item.title: President, CEO of Utah Olympic Legacy Foundation dies at 58
item.description: The Utah Olympic Legacy Foundation announced that longtime President and CEO Colin Hilton died Friday at age 58, after leading the organization for two decades and helping sustain the legacy of Utah's 2002 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games. Hilton also worked closely with Utah 2034, the group preparing for the 2034 Winter Games, and Utah 2034 CEO Brad Wilson said he was heartbroken, crediting Hilton with turning the 2002 Games' legacy into something that still serves athletes and communities. The foundation's board named COO Calum Clark acting president and CEO; Clark called Hilton a mentor, boss and friend. The family asked for privacy regarding the circumstances of his death, and no further details were released.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr

item.title: 'Getting worse': Riverton woman sounds call to aid Ukraine after 10th humanitarian trip to country
item.description: Riverton resident Mindie Packer returned this month from her 10th humanitarian trip to Ukraine with her group Hope Across Borders, a 12-day visit from July 21 to Aug. 2 during which the team provided funds, beds, a washer and other aid to 10 displaced Ukrainian families and visited orphanages and refugee centers. Packer said conditions in Ukraine feel worse than a year ago even as U.S. attention and aid appear to be waning, and she's urging people to press Congress for continued sanctions on Russia and military aid. Fellow travelers Julie Benson and Mike Thaller, on their second and fifth trips respectively, described hearing the Ukrainian national anthem played daily and seeing memorials to fallen soldiers, calling the ongoing war "very tragic and melancholy" even as they see resilience among Ukrainians.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack

item.title: 150 companies form coalition in Utah to get defense technology to troops faster
item.description: About 150 mostly small and midsize American companies, many veteran-owned, launched the Integrated Warfighter Ecosystem Friday at Payson-based CenCore's new 55,000-square-foot global headquarters, aiming to speed defense technology to U.S. troops. CenCore CEO Adam Fife said the roughly 18-month-old effort seeks to bridge the "Valley of Death" gap where emerging technology stalls awaiting federal acquisition funding, with about half of member companies new to working with the Department of War. Gov. Spencer Cox and former acting Defense Secretary Chris Miller headlined the launch; Provo-based Hypercraft CEO Brian Bowers said the coalition is already connecting Utah defense firms, including drone and counter-drone companies relevant to lessons from Ukraine. Fife said the goal is to grow the ecosystem to 300 companies within a year.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson

item.title: 'It started out as a dream': Beaver outdoor adventure store closing after disasters in area
item.description: Tucker High Adventure Tours in Beaver, which has offered mountain biking, climbing, hiking and ski tours near the Tushar Mountains since 2017, is closing its brick-and-mortar store after wildfire and flooding destroyed or cut off access to properties owner Mark Tucker's family managed for extra income. Tucker said the business, his oldest son's sole source of income, is holding a fire-and-flood liquidation sale through early September but plans to keep offering tours without the storefront. Ruby's Inn general manager Lance Syrett said nearby Bryce Canyon has seen a smaller outdoor-recreation downturn tied to reduced international travel and other economic factors, even though Utah's outdoor recreation economy supported about 75,000 jobs as of 2024 data.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown

item.title: With 'Super El Niño' on the way, Vail Resorts announces opening dates in the West
item.description: Vail Resorts announced 2026-27 season opening dates for its western resorts, including a Nov. 20 target for Park City Mountain in Utah, as forecasters anticipate a "Super El Niño" winter; Keystone in Colorado aims to open first in October. Utah's independently owned Brian Head Resort, targeting a Nov. 6 opening, spent $1 million on snowmaking upgrades including a new pipeline for up to 24 simultaneous snow guns. NOAA gives an 81% chance of a very strong El Niño this fall and 97% odds it persists through early spring 2027; OpenSnow forecaster Evan Thayer said such patterns typically favor above-average snowfall in southern Utah but a slower, more uncertain start in northern Utah's Wasatch, though he noted the historically strongest El Niño winter (1982-83) delivered 800-900 inches to the Cottonwoods.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Romboy, Deseret News

item.title: How a smashed cuke salad — and other homegrown dishes — are helping fight hunger at Utah Valley University
item.description: Utah Valley University's campus food pantry, part of its Care Hub, served more than 12,000 people and gave away over 67,000 pounds of food last year, including nearly 16,000 pounds of fresh produce grown in its quarter-acre GRIT Garden, according to pantry manager Amber McGuire. To help students who don't know how to use fresh produce, UVU runs "Pantry to Plate" cooking classes — recently teaching a smashed cucumber salad — pairing garden harvests with pantry staples like dried beans and rice in winter. A Utah State University survey found nearly half of Utah college students report some food insecurity, and McGuire said causes range from unexpected expenses to students sleeping in cars or fleeing unsafe housing; other Utah schools including the University of Utah, Salt Lake Community College, BYU, Weber State, Southern Utah University, Utah Tech, Snow College and Westminster all run similar food-assistance programs.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: 'Local watering hole': BYU students pay tribute to gas stations in 'Rest Stop' art show
item.description: Ten BYU art students, guided by professors Madeline Rupard and Christopher Lynn, created "Rest Stop," a gas-station-themed art exhibit displayed Aug. 3-8 at Will's Canyon Stop in Orem, drawing more than 600 visitors. After a road trip studying art theorists and roadside artworks from Boise to Las Vegas, students built a small structure with architect Eric Edvalson to house pieces exploring gas stations as modern rest stops, including a miniature canyon diorama by Ron Rosario and charcoal drawings by Julie Bielefeldt inspired by a friend's memory of his grandfather's station. Rupard said hosting art at a working gas station created an unpredictable energy and exposed the students' work to people who might not otherwise see an art show; she hopes to help students stage a similar show at another gas station in the future.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom

item.title: Reduction of Grand Staircase-Escalante applauded; better stewardship of the land urged
item.description: Locals near the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, including rancher Link Chynoweth, say the 1996 designation drew disruptive tourism to land that was already well cared for, and many welcome a recent reduction of the monument's boundaries. Garfield County Commission Chairman Leland Pollock argues the smaller monument still keeps land protected under the Bureau of Land Management while letting local governments clear drying vegetation that fuels wildfires, calling it a move toward healthier land rather than 2 million acres of undifferentiated sagebrush. Grocery store owner Kevin Griffin says the areas that most need protecting can now get more focused attention, and pushes back on the idea that residents are evenly split on the issue. Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah Chairwoman Laurel Yellowhorse counters that her tribe's connection to the land predates the monument, Utah statehood and the United States itself, warning the reduction risks irreversible damage to cultural resources, ancestral sites and traditional uses.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson

item.title: John Curtis wants to hear any ideas for saving the Great Salt Lake — even the 'stupid' ones
item.description: Sen. John Curtis convened a panel of experts and policymakers to brainstorm ways to save the Great Salt Lake, encouraging them to pitch ideas without fear of judgment and comparing the effort to pioneers' "bold and audacious" water diversion projects. Proposals included expanded cloud-seeding to boost rainfall over the lake and an interstate water pipeline, potentially trading water access with Louisiana in exchange for help with that state's coastal erosion. Curtis was especially interested in technology to cut evaporation from mineral mining operations and in recovering "stranded" desert groundwater west of the lake, though federal land use and unexploded ordnance complicate that idea. He's also working with Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins and Interior subcommittee chair Lisa Murkowski, who back President Trump's proposed $1 billion Great Salt Lake initiative, on securing funding, and says bringing colleagues to see the lake in person would build political support for restoration.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko

item.title: Roy, Riverdale officials consider shifting fire protection to Weber Fire District
item.description: Roy and Riverdale are weighing whether to hand their fire departments over to the Weber Fire District, which already serves eight other Weber County communities, with both cities' facilities, staff and equipment being absorbed and their standalone departments dissolved. Riverdale's city attorney said consolidation would improve coverage when personnel are out sick or on vacation, and the Fire District's chief noted a larger district can better afford specialized equipment that smaller cities can't justify alone. Roy (about 39,000 residents) and Riverdale (about 9,000) each formally declared intent to annex into the district last June, held public hearings in July, and could see the change take effect in January pending sign-off from the Utah Lieutenant Governor's Office. Residents would see municipal property taxes drop but gain a new fire-district line item, estimated around $360 a year for an average Riverdale home and $314 for an average Roy home; officials also noted Riverdale's heavy- and water-rescue specialties would strengthen the countywide district.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack

item.title: Turning Point USA announces memorial at UVU on anniversary of Kirk's assassination
item.description: Turning Point USA will hold a "Freedom Built to Last" memorial on Sept. 10 at Utah Valley University's UCCU Center, marking one year since founder Charlie Kirk was assassinated at that venue during his "All-American Comeback Tour." Announced speakers include Glenn Beck, Frank Turek, Andrew Sypher and Caleb Chilcutt, several of whom were present when Kirk was killed or were close associates. UVU clarified that although campus operations close for the day, the UCCU Center itself remains available for the privately organized event, after some campus outlets initially reported the university had withdrawn support. The university is separately weighing a permanent on-campus memorial, having received several statue proposals that haven't been made public, and organizers plan a nationwide church-invitation initiative starting Sept. 13 tied to Kirk's Christian faith. The murder case against accused shooter Tyler Robinson continues in Utah courts, with a ruling on trial proceedings expected Sept. 1.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco

item.title: Utah 988 lifeline sees summer increase in calls, says it maintains 90% answer rate
item.description: Utah's 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, run by the Huntsman Mental Health Institute, says it's fielding a summer surge in calls — around 400 a day — while still hitting its target 90% answer rate, even as some other states' crisis centers, like one in Los Angeles, have had to reroute calls due to overwhelming demand. A Huntsman crisis line manager said missed calls are typically callers hanging up before staff can answer, and that call volume spikes around 9 a.m. and again from 4 p.m. to 2 a.m., with calls running slightly longer in summer. Huntsman handles all Utah 988 traffic plus overflow calls routed from other states' nearest available centers, and staff assess each caller's risk of self-harm rather than tracking specific reasons for the call. Beyond 988, Huntsman also runs Utah's state crisis line and a peer-support Warm Line for ongoing mental health needs, both offered alongside 988 as 24/7 resources for people in crisis or their concerned friends and family.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton

item.title: Feds establish goal for Lake Powell elevations with finalized 2-year plan
item.description: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum signed a record of decision finalizing the Bureau of Reclamation's Post-2026 Colorado River Operations plan, aiming to stop Lake Powell's decline after the reservoir hit its lowest recorded level earlier this month. The 10-year plan sets biannual elevation targets based on hydrology, calling for Lake Powell to hold around 3,510 feet in 2027-2028 — a bit over 9 feet below its current level — while continuing releases of up to 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to help prop up Powell's levels into next year. Upper Basin states including Utah avoided mandatory water cuts under the plan, while Lower Basin states must together cut 1.25 million acre-feet annually (Arizona 760,000, California 444,000, Nevada 50,000 acre-feet), with actual release amounts to be set in April 2027 once winter snowpack projections firm up. Utah Gov. Spencer Cox said he wants to keep Powell from reaching "deadpool" status but would prefer a longer-term interstate agreement over the federal plan, while California signaled openness to flexibility for Upper Basin states in exchange for what it called "robust action" on their water use.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams

item.title: Cause determined for Canyon Road Fire in Logan
item.description: State officials have determined that the Canyon Road Fire, which broke out July 31 near Utah State University and burned just over 17 acres of state land, was caused by spontaneous combustion of organic material — the same process that can ignite improperly dried hay bales or yard-waste piles. Logan City Fire Marshal Aaron Walker said the fire started on state property below the city and, despite its relatively small size, raised safety concerns because of its closeness to homes as flames spread through dry vegetation. Walker is urging homeowners to spread out organic debris piles, monitor them for heat buildup, keep combustibles away from structures and have water sources readily accessible, in line with the "Ready, Set, Go" wildfire-preparedness program's push for defensible space and clearing combustibles within five feet of homes. Cache County has since raised its fire restrictions to Level 2, banning open flames, and officials say fire danger remains high around Logan despite recent rain because of continued heat, wind and dry grass.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz

item.title: Odyssey Elementary Family Resource Center helps families start the school year
item.description: Odyssey Elementary in Ogden, the boundary school for a local homeless shelter, runs a Family Resource Center offering families a kitchen and food pantry, dining and living space, showers, laundry, and a clothing closet ahead of the new school year. Principal Sonja Davidson said the center is meant to be a resource hub for families, while community school coordinator Destiny De Herrera said it addresses needs that have grown throughout her career in the district. As a Title I school, all students at Odyssey already receive free breakfast and lunch, and similar teen centers operate at area high schools. Organizers say removing these barriers lets students focus on learning, and the Ogden School Foundation's website accepts donations to support the effort.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer

item.title: Grass fire in Garland prompts I-15 closure, neighborhood evacuation
item.description: A wildfire dubbed the Harley Fire broke out Friday afternoon near Garland in Box Elder County, prompting the Garland Fire Department to evacuate residents along Harley Drive. Utah Highway Patrol Lt. Zach Randall confirmed I-15 was closed in both directions at the Riverside exit as crews responded, with UDOT initially estimating the roadway would reopen around 6:40 p.m. Utah Fire Info reported the blaze had burned an estimated 75 acres and was threatening structures along with power lines, roads and water infrastructure. Officials urged nearby residents to follow evacuation orders immediately and to steer clear of the area while firefighting continued.
item.dc:creator: Payton Davis

item.title: Governor says efforts to reduce Utah's housing prices aren't working
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox acknowledged during his monthly news conference that state efforts to rein in Utah's housing costs haven't worked, as Salt Lake County's median single-family home price hit a record $645,000. Cox set a 2023 goal of building 35,000 starter homes by 2028, but only about 7,400 have been completed so far, something he called "really, really hard to hit." He said the fundamental issue is that demand keeps outpacing supply, and pointed to strategies involving state-owned land and postal service property as ways he's still trying to boost the housing stock, even though he can't control every market factor. University of Utah housing analyst Dejan Eskic and Sen. John Curtis were also referenced in coverage of the state's ongoing affordability challenges, with Utah's unemployment rate holding at 3.6%.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff

item.title: Proposed high-rise next to Salt Lake City historic church quietly fizzles
item.description: A proposed 225-foot, 421-unit mixed-use high-rise next to St. Mark's Cathedral in Salt Lake City's Central City neighborhood has fallen apart after the property was sold in May. Silverado Building Company had sought a rezone for the site at 265 E. 100 South starting in 2024, winning Planning Commission approval in fall 2025 despite objections over seismic risk to the historic 1871 church and its solar panels; the plan called for 20% affordable units and ground-floor commercial space. The Salt Lake City Council paused its rezone vote in early 2026 after a contentious public hearing and the item never returned to the agenda before buyer APWireless Infrastructure Partners finalized the purchase. Travis Starley of the Central City Neighborhood Council said residents are "ecstatic" the tower fell through and hope whatever comes next respects the church next door.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams

item.title: Utah barbershop chain helps with back-to-school through backpack donations
item.description: The Fellas Chop Shop, a Utah barbershop chain co-founded in 2018 by Jeramy Reber and his wife Mersadies, is collecting donations to hand out 250 backpacks filled with school supplies to students in need. The drive, tied to celebrating America's 250th birthday, lets customers donate supplies or money at any location, or buy shop products with proceeds going toward the effort. At the Spanish Fork shop, client Tyler DeCapot said he learned about the drive during a beard trim and wanted to help spread the word, while barber Jaron Bradford also voiced support. Reber said the goal is to be part of the communities the shop serves and to help level the playing field for underprivileged students heading back to class.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams

item.title: Firefighting costs in Utah projected to hit record level this year
item.description: Utah is on pace to spend a record $300 million fighting wildfires in 2026, up from $240 million in 2025, with the state's share running around $45 million, according to Wade Snyder, deputy fire manager for the Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands. Costs are split among the state, U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management. Nearly 900 wildfires have burned more than 527,000 acres so far this year, making it Utah's second-worst fire season on record behind 2007's roughly 629,000 acres, driven by extremely dry conditions after a low-snow winter and costly early timber fires near communities. Snyder said the state's wildfire fund currently covers suppression and some recovery work — the first year it's been authorized for post-suppression rehabilitation — but warned legislative funding could fall short if severe fire seasons keep recurring.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff

item.title: Utah economy holding steady, sentiment increasing despite challenges
item.description: Utah's job market and consumer sentiment both showed resilience in July, according to the Utah Department of Workforce Services and Zions Bank. Non-farm payroll employment rose 1.4% over the past year, adding 25,200 jobs, while the state's seasonally adjusted unemployment rate held at 3.6% (64,800 Utahns unemployed), well below the national rate of 4.1%. Chief economist Ben Crabb pointed to that as a sign of labor market resilience. Zions Bank's Consumer Sentiment survey found Utah's index rose 1.8% in July to 72.7, versus 55.2 nationally, though both remain down from a year ago (Utah -7.2%, U.S. -10.5%) after a sharp April drop. Zions Bank chief economist Robert Spendlove cited growing optimism, with Utah's one-year financial outlook index climbing from 102 in June to 111 in July, even as gas prices in the state averaged $4.37 a gallon, more than 25 cents above the national average and over a dollar higher than a year ago.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich

item.title: 'Because of him': North Capitol building named in honor of former Utah Gov. Mike Leavitt
item.description: Utah's North Capitol building was officially dedicated Friday as the Michael O. Leavitt Building, honoring the state's 14th governor, who served from 1993 to 2003. Gov. Spencer Cox, Senate President Stuart Adams, House Majority Whip Candice Pierucci, former U.S. Sen. Mitt Romney and Leavitt himself attended the Capitol ceremony; Leavitt's parents, ages 97 and 94, watched remotely. Cox called it the "rarest of circumstances" to name a building after a living person. The $320 million building opened earlier this year and houses the Museum of Utah, which opened its exhibits in June, along with a large stained-glass laylight depicting all 29 Utah counties. Speakers credited Leavitt's tenure with steering the successful 2002 Salt Lake City Winter Olympics — for which he tapped Romney to lead the organizing committee — laying an economic foundation for the state's growth, and later serving as EPA administrator under President George W. Bush.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko

item.title: Former employee accused of stealing from Utah airline, then faking death
item.description: Felix Odiott Beltran, 39, a former Breeze Airways employee, was charged Friday in 3rd District Court with theft by deception and attempted theft by deception. Prosecutors say Beltran was placed on unpaid suspension in early December for misconduct, then used his still-active access to the payroll system to add 196 fraudulent work hours, netting a $6,808.85 direct deposit. After Breeze fired him on Dec. 29, he allegedly logged into payroll again the same day and added another 196 hours, but the company caught and blocked that second payment. When Breeze sent a demand letter in January seeking repayment, it received a reply claiming Beltran had died by suicide. Salt Lake City police say they confirmed in July, through a relative, that Beltran was alive and had relocated to Florida.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy

item.title: Utah Gov. Cox on the banana fallacy and nuclear safety
item.description: At his monthly press conference Thursday, Gov. Spencer Cox defended the state's nuclear-energy billboard campaign after three groups — including Downwinders Inc. and Utah Physicians for a Healthy Environment — filed an FTC complaint calling ads like "nuclear plants emit less radiation than bananas" misleading. Cox said reception to nuclear power in Utah has been "overwhelmingly positive" and accused critics of selectively following science, tying the pushback to his Operation Gigawatt push to roughly double the state's electricity generation capacity by 2034 through nuclear, geothermal and solar projects. He also addressed backlash over President Trump's July 13 reduction of two Utah national monuments by about 3 million combined acres, citing new Deseret News-Hinckley Institute polling showing 56% of Utah voters opposed the move but 82% want state, local or county governments — not the federal government — to have the most say over how public lands are managed. Cox argued the monument rollback reflects that preference for local control rather than a sell-off of protected land, and said Utah is coordinating with federal nuclear regulators to ensure safety as new energy projects move forward.
item.dc:creator: Eva Terry, Deseret News

item.title: Here's how to get reservations for the Salt Lake Temple Open House
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints will open ticket reservations Sept. 1 at 11 a.m. on TempleSquare.org and the Temple Square app for the Salt Lake Temple Celebration, running April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027. Individuals can request up to six tour tickets, while larger groups submit separate reservation requests; tours run 8:40 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily, with Sunday hours starting at noon. The church expects millions of guests and says reservations are recommended but not required for most celebration activities beyond the temple tour itself, and virtual participation will be offered worldwide. Additional ticket releases are planned if preferred dates are unavailable after the initial Sept. 1 opening. The celebration marks the reopening of the church's renovated flagship temple and will include exhibits and experiences beyond the tour.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft

item.title: 'Game changer': Cancer center opens at Park City Hospital
item.description: Park City Hospital celebrated a ribbon-cutting Thursday for a new cancer center that began seeing patients Friday, expanding infusion capacity from 4 to 18 chairs and adding radiation therapy technology for a region spanning Summit and Wasatch counties, the Uintah Basin and parts of neighboring states. Surgical oncologist Tawnya Bowles called the on-site radiation therapy a "game changer" for patients who need daily treatment over six-week courses, while hospital president Lori Weston said the center allows coordinated, personalized cancer care without leaving the community. Midway patient Jim Becker, who previously drove two hours each way five days a week for treatment, and nurse-and-patient Dani Kurtz both spoke at the opening about the toll of long-distance care. Medical oncologist Clarke Low said patients deserve world-class care close to home, and hospital leaders noted the center will also offer survivorship support including nutrition, mental health and financial navigation services.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft

item.title: Juab County employee accused of misusing public money
item.description: Kristin Rose Miller, 37, of Nephi, was charged Friday in 4th District Court with misusing public money, a third-degree felony, over her use of a Juab County-issued credit card. Prosecutors say a February review found roughly $1,600 in charges Miller acknowledged were personal and promised to repay, but never did; a similar pattern turned up in March and April purchases lacking receipts or explanations despite her having signed an acknowledgment of the card policy in March. Miller, hired as county administrator in January, reportedly stalled when asked to account for the charges, at one point blaming her county card being linked to her Apple Wallet, and by late April had documented only 2 of about 70 March purchases. Investigators also flagged additional questionable charges on a separate fire district credit card.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy

item.title: Here's how much it would cost to attend a college football game in Utah
item.description: A new analysis of ticket prices for Utah's three FBS programs — the University of Utah, BYU and Utah State — finds a wide range in what fans pay to attend a game this season. The cheapest single-game ticket, for Utah's matchup against Idaho, runs $38, while the priciest seats climb sharply for marquee matchups: BYU's cheapest ticket against Utah is $331, and a seat for BYU vs. Notre Dame runs about $600. For a family of four at a typical non-marquee game, estimated costs come to roughly $425 at BYU, $340 at Utah and $185 at Utah State. A companion poll of 789 registered Utah voters found 56% consider themselves avid or casual football fans, but nearly a third say attending games is unaffordable — including half of those earning under $50,000 a year, compared with only about 10% of fans aged 45-64 who call it very affordable. The piece attributes rising costs to post-pandemic demand, NIL deals, revenue sharing, an expanded College Football Playoff and general inflation.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Romboy, Deseret News

item.title: While Salt Lake immigrant detention center plans are dead, talk of finding a site may not be over
item.description: Federal officials have officially scrapped plans to convert a Salt Lake City warehouse into a large-scale immigrant detention center, according to a Wednesday court filing that says the property will instead be declared surplus for disposal by the General Services Administration. Gov. Spencer Cox said at his monthly press conference that conversations about siting a detention facility somewhere in Utah are still happening, even though no location has been identified. Immigrant-rights attorney Jim McConkie, who had been preparing a lawsuit with the group Uproar Utah to block the Salt Lake City site, doubts the debate is over and suspects federal officials could pursue a smaller facility in southern Utah instead. ICE had paid $145.44 million for the 300 South warehouse last year before Salt Lake City and Salt Lake County sued to block the conversion. McConkie also predicted continued aggressive immigration enforcement under new DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and said attorneys are weighing legal challenges against Utah law enforcement agencies with 287(g) cooperation agreements with ICE.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Logan businesses donate 1,500 meals to firefighters, commemorating 2 fallen officers
item.description: Three Logan businesses — Romo's Mediterranean Grill & Market, K9s Unleashed Training Academy and Big Deal Outlet — donated about 1,500 emergency meals to the Logan City Fire Department, which has been distributing them to firefighters across Cache and Box Elder counties. Romo's owner Steve Romo said he and his wife wanted to honor Tremonton-Garland police officers Eric Estrada and Sgt. Lee Sorensen, who were killed responding to a domestic violence call on Aug. 17, 2025, timing the gift near the anniversary of their deaths. Logan Fire EMS Assistant Chief Andy Shock, a 23-year department veteran, called the donation both unexpected and meaningful and said the community-funded meals are going out to firefighters, including those battling wildland fires. Romo said the gesture reflects the close-knit relationships between business owners and first responders in Cache County.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Everyone's talking about a 'super El Niño' winter, but how will it affect Utah's fall?
item.description: The National Weather Service's Climate Prediction Center's fall outlook, released Thursday, favors above-normal precipitation across most of Utah for September through November, with above-normal temperatures also more likely, according to KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson. A strengthening El Niño pattern — now given a 90% chance of becoming "very strong" this winter — has already contributed to an unusually wet monsoon season, including Utah's 31st-wettest July on record. Southeast Utah has the best odds for above-normal fall precipitation, while northwest Utah's chances are closer to neutral, and forecasters caution the outlook says nothing about how far above or below normal conditions could land. Utah's reservoirs, now at 52% capacity after a record-low snowpack, won't be fixed by fall rain alone, but healthy fall soil moisture helps next spring's snowpack melt more efficiently. Gov. Spencer Cox said Thursday he's hopeful El Niño delivers a strong winter, warning that another bad year would mean tighter water restrictions.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Aging Utahns struggling with property taxes can qualify for up to $1200
item.description: AARP is highlighting Utah's little-known Circuit Breaker Tax Relief program, which can pay homeowners 66 or older (or their surviving spouses) up to $1,200 a year, with the benefit shrinking as household income rises toward the roughly $45,000 cutoff. "It's sometimes between groceries or medication or property tax," said AARP's Joseph Hirabayashi, who noted a separate renter refund is also available. Homeowners apply through their county by Sept. 1, while renters have until Dec. 31 to apply through the Utah State Tax Commission.
item.dc:creator: Tamara Vaifanua, KSL

item.title: New schools make room for Davis County's growing student population
item.description: Davis School District has opened Horizon Junior High, Island View Elementary and, this year, Still Water Elementary to keep pace with growth as families move into the county.
